name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MATCH_Q01 - Theories and scientists of origin of life

questiontext.text:
Match the theories or scientists in the left column with their corresponding concepts in the right column:

List-I List-II
A. Big Bang theory (i) Units of life called spores transferred from outer space
B. Panspermia (ii) First life arose from non-living organic molecules via chemical evolution
C. Louis Pasteur (iii) Singular huge explosion explaining the origin of the universe
D. Oparin and Haldane (iv) Disproved spontaneous generation using pre-sterilised flasks

Select the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Understanding the origin of life requires distinguishing cosmological theories of the universe's origin from biological and chemical hypotheses for how life first appeared on Earth.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Concept
- The Big Bang theory explains the origin of the universe through a singular huge explosion unimaginable in physical terms, followed by expansion and cooling.
- Panspermia is the idea favoured by early Greek thinkers and some astronomers that units of life called spores were transferred to different planets including Earth.
- Louis Pasteur demonstrated experimentally using pre-sterilised flasks and killed yeast that life comes only from pre-existing life, dismissing spontaneous generation.
- Oparin and Haldane proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules and that formation of life was preceded by chemical evolution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Big Bang theory with singular huge explosion explaining the origin of the universe; Panspermia with units of life called spores transferred from outer space; Louis Pasteur with disproved spontaneous generation using pre-sterilised flasks; and Oparin and Haldane with first life arose from non-living organic molecules via chemical evolution, giving the combination A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MATCH_Q02 - Evidences for evolution and evolutionary phenomena

questiontext.text:
Match the evolutionary observations with their corresponding evolutionary concepts or evidences:

List-I List-II
A. Forelimbs of whale and bat (i) Disapproved by Karl Ernst von Baer
B. Eyes of octopus and mammals (ii) Divergent evolution (homologous structures)
C. Ernst Haeckel's embryological proposal (iii) Paleontological evidence
D. Fossils in sedimentary rock layers (iv) Convergent evolution (analogous structures)

Select the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Evidence for evolution comes from paleontology, comparative embryology, and comparative anatomy (homology and analogy).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Concept
- Forelimbs of whale and bat share the same basic bone pattern (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges) adapted for different functions, representing divergent evolution and homologous structures.
- Eyes of octopus and mammals have different anatomical origins but perform the same function of vision, representing convergent evolution and analogous structures.
- Ernst Haeckel's embryological proposal (that vertebrate embryos share features absent in adults) was disapproved by Karl Ernst von Baer, who noted embryos never pass through adult stages of other animals.
- Fossils in sedimentary rock layers indicate the geological periods in which different extinct organisms existed, constituting paleontological evidence.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MATCH_Q03 - Convergent evolution of placental and marsupial mammals

questiontext.text:
Match the placental mammals with their corresponding Australian marsupial counterparts exhibiting convergent evolution:

List-I (Placental Mammals) List-II (Australian Marsupials)
A. Anteater (i) Flying phalanger
B. Lemur (ii) Numbat
C. Flying squirrel (iii) Tasmanian tiger cat
D. Bobcat (iv) Spotted cuscus

Select the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When more than one adaptive radiation occurs in an isolated geographical area such as Australia, placental mammals and Australian marsupials evolve into forms that resemble each other due to similar ecological niches, illustrating convergent evolution.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- The placental Anteater corresponds to the Australian marsupial Numbat.
- The placental Lemur corresponds to the Australian marsupial Spotted cuscus.
- The placental Flying squirrel corresponds to the Australian marsupial Flying phalanger.
- The placental Bobcat corresponds to the Australian marsupial Tasmanian tiger cat.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MATCH_Q04 - Naturalists and their evolutionary concepts

questiontext.text:
Match the naturalists/scientists with their respective contributions or concepts in evolutionary biology:

List-I List-II
A. Charles Darwin (i) Worked in Malay Archipelago and reached conclusions similar to natural selection
B. Alfred Wallace (ii) Proposed saltation (single-step large mutation) causing speciation
C. Lamarck (iii) Proposed branching descent and natural selection as key concepts
D. Hugo de Vries (iv) Proposed evolution driven by use and disuse of organs

Select the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different scientists proposed distinct mechanisms to explain how species evolve over time.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Scientist
- Charles Darwin based his theory of evolution on two key concepts: branching descent and natural selection.
- Alfred Wallace was a naturalist who worked in the Malay Archipelago and independently arrived at conclusions similar to Darwin's around the same time.
- Lamarck, a French naturalist, proposed that evolution occurred due to the use and disuse of organs, citing the elongation of giraffe necks as an example.
- Hugo de Vries, working on evening primrose, proposed that large, random, directionless mutations called saltation (single-step large mutation) cause speciation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MATCH_Q05 - Factors affecting Hardy-Weinberg genetic equilibrium

questiontext.text:
Match the evolutionary terms related to Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with their correct descriptions:

List-I List-II
A. Gene flow (i) Original drifted population becomes founders of a new species
B. Genetic drift (ii) Gene migration occurring multiple times between populations
C. Founder effect (iii) Natural selection where more individuals acquire the mean character value
D. Stabilising selection (iv) Change in allele frequency occurring by chance

Select the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium states that allele frequencies remain constant across generations unless disturbed by evolutionary factors such as gene migration/flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination, or natural selection.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
- Gene flow occurs when gene migration (movement of a section of population to another place) happens multiple times, altering allele frequencies in both the original and new populations.
- Genetic drift refers to a change in allele frequency that occurs purely by chance.
- Founder effect occurs when the change in allele frequency in a drifted sample is so distinct that they become a different species, with the original drifted population acting as founders.
- Stabilising selection is a mode of natural selection in which more individuals acquire the mean character value, making the distribution peak higher and narrower.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MATCH_Q06 - Geological timeline of major evolutionary events

questiontext.text:
Match the major evolutionary events with their approximate time of occurrence:

List-I (Evolutionary Event) List-II (Approximate Time)
A. First cellular forms of life appeared on Earth (i) 500 mya
B. Invertebrates were formed and active (ii) 200 mya
C. Jawless fish and lobefins evolved (iii) 2000 mya
D. Land reptiles returned to water to evolve into fish-like reptiles (Ichthyosaurus) (iv) 350 mya

Select the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The brief account of evolution traces the sequential appearance of cellular life, invertebrates, early vertebrates, and marine reptiles across millions of years ago (mya).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Event
- The first cellular forms of life appeared on Earth about 2000 mya.
- Invertebrates were formed and became active by about 500 mya.
- Jawless fish probably evolved around 350 mya, and fish with stout and strong fins (lobefins) could move on land and return to water around 350 mya.
- Some land reptiles went back into water to evolve into fish-like reptiles such as Ichthyosaurus probably around 200 mya.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MATCH_Q07 - Evolutionary significance of ancient plant and vertebrate taxa

questiontext.text:
Match the ancestral or extinct organisms with their evolutionary significance:

List-I List-II
A. Lobefins (Coelacanth) (i) Fell slowly to form coal deposits
B. Tyrannosaurus rex (ii) Evolved into the first amphibians, ancestors of modern frogs and salamanders
C. Giant ferns (Pteridophytes) (iii) Reptilian lineage that gave rise to dinosaurs, crocodiles, and birds
D. Sauropsids (iv) Biggest land dinosaur, about 20 feet in height with dagger-like teeth

Select the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Fossil records and evolutionary lineages connect ancient organisms to modern descendants or geological formations.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Organism
- Lobefins (such as the Coelacanth caught in South Africa in 1938) were fish with stout, strong fins that evolved into the first amphibians, the ancestors of modern-day frogs and salamanders.
- Tyrannosaurus rex was the largest of the land dinosaurs, standing about 20 feet in height with huge fearsome dagger-like teeth.
- Giant ferns (pteridophytes) were abundant in earlier eras and fell slowly to form coal deposits.
- Sauropsids represent the major reptilian lineage that gave rise to turtles, lizards, snakes, dinosaurs, crocodiles, and birds (whereas Synapsids gave rise to mammals).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MATCH_Q08 - Brain capacities and traits in human evolution

questiontext.text:
Match the primates/hominids with their characteristic brain capacities or evolutionary traits:

List-I List-II
A. Dryopithecus (i) Brain capacity 650–800 cc; probably did not eat meat
B. Homo habilis (ii) Brain capacity 1400 cc; used hides and buried their dead
C. Homo erectus (iii) More ape-like primate existing about 15 mya
D. Neanderthal man (iv) Brain capacity around 900 cc; fossils discovered in Java in 1891

Select the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Human evolution is characterised by progressive changes in posture, cranial capacity, tool use, and cultural practices.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Hominid/Primate
- Dryopithecus existed about 15 mya alongside Ramapithecus; Dryopithecus was more ape-like whereas Ramapithecus was more man-like.
- Homo habilis was the first human-like hominid with a brain capacity of 650–800 cc and probably did not eat meat.
- Homo erectus, whose fossils were discovered in Java in 1891 (dating to about 1.5 mya), had a large brain around 900 cc and probably ate meat.
- Neanderthal man had a brain size of 1400 cc, lived in the Near East and Central Asia between 1,00,000–40,000 years ago, used hides to protect the body, and buried their dead.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EVOLUTION_MATCH_Q09 - Timeline of Earth origin and human evolution

questiontext.text:
Match the milestones in Earth's history and human evolution with their approximate ages:

List-I (Milestone) List-II (Approximate Time)
A. Formation of Earth (i) 75,000–10,000 years ago
B. Australopithecines in East African grasslands (ii) 4.5 billion years ago
C. Modern Homo sapiens arose during ice age (iii) About 18,000 years ago
D. Pre-historic cave art (e.g., Bhimbetka rock shelter) (iv) 2 million years ago

Select the correct matching combination:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Geological and anthropological timelines place the formation of Earth in billions of years ago, early hominids in millions of years ago, and modern human cultural milestones in tens of thousands of years ago.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Milestone
- Formation of Earth in the solar system of the Milky Way galaxy occurred about 4.5 billion years ago.
- Australopithecines probably lived in East African grasslands about 2 million years ago, hunting with stone weapons and essentially eating fruit.
- Modern Homo sapiens arose during the ice age between 75,000–10,000 years ago.
- Pre-historic cave art, such as the paintings at Bhimbetka rock shelter in Madhya Pradesh, developed about 18,000 years ago.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching combination is A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(iii).
